_comment: The applications the demo site is built from, and what each one is
supposed to print. One entry here is the whole of adding a build: it
feeds scripts/stage_site.sh, the _site/manifest.json the page reads its
menu from, and scripts/check_site.mjs, which is what CI runs.
app: a path under the west workspace. {module} is this repository.
expect: substrings that must all appear in the output. This is the
acceptance criterion, so it should name what the application is for,
not merely that it started.
endless: the application never finishes, so the harness gives up at
max_time_ms and exits 2. Expected, not a failure.
title: a short name for the menu. hint: one sentence the page shows
while it runs, saying what it does or what to do. Both required.
uses: what of the board the page should show: leds, buttons, flash
(the Erase flash button), terminal (the output reads the keyboard: a
cursor, and keys go to the guest's UART), accel (the Tilt pad, which
sets what the emulated accelerometer reads). A display build is marked by
display instead. Checked against each build's .config.
interactive: the application waits for a person. The page forwards
keystrokes on the output to the guest's UART.
clock: virtual (default) or paced. Paced lets virtual time pass at the
rate it claims, so a sample that blinks once a second can be watched.
The page honours it; the checks do not, because the guest sees the
same clock either way and waiting would only make CI slower. Every
interactive build is paced, so a person sees real timestamps and the
guest does not race ahead while waiting for them.
max_time_ms is what the page gives a build; ci_max_time_ms overrides it
for the checks, which have no one watching.
ci_gpio: scripted input-pin events, so a sample that waits for a
button can be checked unattended and deterministically.
upstream: unmodified upstream Zephyr code. false for this port's own
tests, which prove the port rather than the samples.
kind: sample or test. The score in ROADMAP.md counts upstream samples,
because the samples are the teaching material. An upstream test suite
is evidence for the port and is not a sample.
persist_expect / persist_absent: for a build that keeps
simulated flash. The browser check runs it, reloads the page and runs
it again: the second run must print persist_expect and must not print
persist_absent, which is what it prints when the flash is empty.
display: the build draws on the board's display, so the page shows its
canvas and check_site.mjs screenshots the last frame, which must show
at least display.colors_at_least distinct colours.
ci_touch: scripted touches, <ms>:<x>,<y> in display pixels: run.mjs
--touch for the Node check, a real click on the canvas for the
browser check.
ci_accel: scripted accelerometer readings, <ms>:<x>,<y>,<z> in m/s^2:
run.mjs --accel for the Node check. The browser check drags the Tilt
pad instead, which cannot land on exact values, so what the script
should produce goes in ci_expect, which only the Node check reads.
args: build arguments, only ever the upstream entry's own extra_configs
(the LVGL demos app chooses its demo that way).
lesson: a guided lesson, as a list of steps the page shows one at a
time, each written like a hint. Nothing checks that a step was
followed; the browser check follows them to see that they still hold.
threads_expect: substrings the thread table must show at some point in
the Node check's run (run.mjs --threads), for a lesson that relies
on what the table says.
boards: two boards joined by an Ethernet link, in place of app. Each
has an app, a label, and what a build has: args (with
-DSNIPPET=wasm-ethernet, which gives it the link), uses, ci_stdin and
expect, which is checked against that board's own output. They are
built as <name>-0 and <name>-1. The page runs them side by side; the
Node check runs them with run.mjs --peer. The link is real-time, so a
pair is paced and its expectations are thresholds.
A board's args may only turn the link on and set addresses, ports and
IP versions (PAIR_ARG in apps.py); overrides says in words what was
set, and the page shows it. start_after_ms powers a board on after the
other, as a client is plugged in after its server; the first board is
the one that starts first. ci_link_frames_at_least is how many frames
the browser check wants each way (default 100).

builds.name: philo
builds.title: Dining philosophers
builds.hint: Six threads contend for forks, forever; the speed control changes their pace.
lesson: Press Run. Six philosophers share six forks, and each philosopher is a thread. The table under the output is the kernel's own list of threads: watch each one think, wait for a fork, and eat.
Press Pause. Nothing runs now, and nothing is lost: every thread keeps its state and its stack. The table is the kernel's answer, asked of the guest between two context switches, not a guess.

Press Step. The kernel runs to its next stop: a context switch, or waking from idle. The arrow marks the thread that holds the CPU. Philosophers 0 to 5 start at priorities 3, 2, 1, 0, -1 and -2, which the output shows as `P:` for preemptible and `C:` for cooperative. The lower number runs first, and a cooperative thread, once running, keeps the CPU until it waits for something.

Find a philosopher whose state is `pending`. The waiting-for column says which fork, a mutex, it is waiting for, and which philosopher holds it. Compare the holder's priority with the one it started at. A mutex lends its owner the priority of the most urgent thread waiting for it, so that the owner finishes and lets go sooner. That is priority inheritance.

Why does this never deadlock? If each philosopher took the fork on one side and then waited for the other, all six could hold one fork each and wait forever. Here each takes the lower-numbered of their two forks first, so Philosopher 5 reaches for fork 0 before fork 5. A circle of waiting would need someone to hold a higher fork while waiting for a lower one, and no one ever does. See `philosopher()` in `samples/philosophers/src/main.c`.

Press Back to undo a step. The whole machine is one block of memory, so the page keeps a copy from before each step and puts it back. Step back to the moment a fork changed hands: the waiter leaves `pending`, and the holder's priority drops back to where it started.

builds.name: logger
builds.title: Logging
builds.hint: Exercises the logging subsystem and exits. Its speed estimate is meaningless here: logging takes no time on a virtual clock, and the sample's 32-bit arithmetic overflows.
expect: RUNNING LOGGER DEMO FROM KERNEL THREAD

builds.title: System heap
builds.hint: Allocates from a sys_heap and prints its statistics.
expect: allocated 156, free 36, max allocated 156, heap size 256

builds.name: metairq
builds.title: Meta-IRQ dispatch
builds.hint: Measures how fast meta-IRQ threads preempt the rest.

builds.name: display
builds.title: Display
builds.hint: Draws upstream's display test pattern on the canvas.

builds.name: touch
builds.title: Touch events
builds.hint: Click or drag on the display to move the crosshair.

builds.name: lvgl
builds.title: LVGL widgets
builds.hint: Click and drag on the display; the output is a shell as well.

builds.name: nvs
builds.title: NVS in flash
builds.hint: Stores values in flash and reboots itself. Run it again — even after reloading the page — and the values are still there; Erase flash starts over.

builds.name: hsm
builds.title: Hierarchical state machine
builds.hint: Click the output, then type `hsm_psicc2 event A` (events A to I).

builds.name: shell
builds.title: Shell
builds.hint: Click the output, then type `help` and press Enter. This sample turns off the boot banner, so it starts at the prompt.

builds.name: echo
builds.title: Echo over Ethernet (two boards)
builds.hint: Two boards on one link: the client echoes TCP and UDP off the server. Type `net iface` or `net ping 192.0.2.2` in the server's terminal.

builds.name: echo-async
builds.title: Echo, asynchronous server (two boards)
builds.hint: echo_client against echo_async, a single-threaded server that serves several clients with poll(). TCP only, so the client's UDP half reports that nothing came back.

builds.name: echo-select
builds.title: Echo, select() server (two boards)
builds.hint: echo_client against echo_async_select, the same server built on select(). TCP only, so the client's UDP half reports that nothing came back.

builds.name: echo-one
builds.title: Echo, one client at a time (two boards)
builds.hint: echo_client against the simplest echo server, which serves one TCP connection at a time. The client connects over IPv6 first, so its IPv4 connection waits in the backlog.

builds.name: coap
builds.title: CoAP client and server (two boards)
builds.hint: coap_client asks coap_server for resources over IPv6: GET, PUT, POST and DELETE, a 2 KB resource in 64-byte blocks, and an observed counter that the server pushes every 5 s.
builds.overrides: The client is given the address 2001:db8::2 and pointed at the server's CoAP port, [2001:db8::1]:5683; as shipped, both boards would be ::1 and the client would look for a server at ::2.

builds.name: coap-up
builds.title: CoAP upload (two boards)
builds.hint: coap_upload sends coap_server four PUTs over IPv6: two short, two in 128-byte blocks, which the server asks to have in 64s.
builds.overrides: The client is given the address 2001:db8::2 and the server's, 2001:db8::1, and its IPv4 is turned off: the server speaks only IPv6, and as shipped the client tries IPv4 first and waits minutes for each timeout.

boards.label: Client
expect: CoAP upload blockwise with callback done in

builds.name: coap-down
builds.title: CoAP download (two boards)
builds.hint: coap_download fetches a 2 KB resource from coap_server over IPv6, 64 bytes at a time.
builds.overrides: The client is given the address 2001:db8::2 and the server's, 2001:db8::1, and its IPv4 is turned off, as for the upload; and it asks for the server's large resource, since the file it names by default is not one coap_server has.

builds.name: http
builds.title: HTTP client and server (two boards)
builds.hint: http_client makes GET and POST requests of http_server over IPv4 and IPv6. The server also has a shell: try `net iface` there.
builds.overrides: The server listens on port 8000, which the client has built in, rather than 80; and the client's addresses are swapped to 192.0.2.2 and 2001:db8::2, with the server as its peer.
